references.text: Aaron died on Mount Hor in the fortieth year after the Israelites had left Egypt, confirming the forty years of wandering in the wilderness.
Moses reminds the people how God humbled them and let them hunger, but then gave them manna to eat in the wilderness to teach them that man does not live by bread alone.
God led the Israelites for forty years in the wilderness, and their clothes and sandals did not wear out.
The manna ceased the day after the Israelites had eaten from the produce of the land in Canaan, marking the end of the forty years of manna.
Nehemiah confirms that God gave the Israelites manna for food and did not withhold it from them during the forty years in the wilderness.
The psalm describes how God let manna rain down on the people and gave them grain from heaven.
God gave the people quail and satisfied them with bread from heaven.
Jesus refers to the manna that the fathers ate in the wilderness and explains that it was the Father who gave them the true bread from heaven.
Jesus contrasts the manna in the wilderness with himself as the bread of life; the fathers ate the manna and died, but whoever eats of him shall live forever.
Stephen mentions the forty years during which Moses led the people in the wilderness with signs and wonders.
Paul notes that God bore with the Israelites in the wilderness for about forty years.
The letter to the Hebrews asks whom God was angry with for forty years—those who sinned and fell in the wilderness.
The hidden manna is mentioned as a promise to the one who overcomes, linking the manna to spiritual nourishment and eternal life.
Describes the historical end of the manna period at the entrance to Canaan, completing the event begun in Exodus.
Uses the manna event as a theological contrast point to highlight Christ's superiority as the eternal bread.
The manna event is explicitly cited to establish a typological parallel to Jesus' role as the bread from heaven.
